title: "Lab 5: Power Analysis"
---

## Packages for Today (Install If Needed)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(pwr)
```
:::



## Overview

The primary package we'll use for conducting power analyses is `pwr`.

Functions we will be using today: 

* `pwr.norm.test`
* `pwr.t.test`
* `pwr.t2n.test`
* `pwr.chisq.test`


## The Logic of the `pwr` Package Functions

Most of the functions of the `pwr` structure work in the same way in that the usually have four main arguments:

- The effect size, `d =`, in the case of *t*-tests.
- The sample size, `n =`
- The type I error rate, `sig.level =`
- The desired power of your experiment, `power =` 

Set one of these four arguments to `NULL` to solve for that value (e.g., `n = NULL` means to solve for sample size).

- Arguments may be named differently depending on the type of power analysis, so always check the function help page. 

 
## Power for $z$-tests

In the case of a *z*-test, to get **power** given effect size, sample size, and desired type I error rate:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.norm.test(d = .5, 
              n = 10, 
              sig.level = .05, 
              power = NULL,
              alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Mean power calculation for normal distribution with known variance 

              d = 0.5
              n = 10
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.3526081
    alternative = two.sided
```


:::
:::



## Power for $z$-tests

To get required **sample size** given effect size, desired type I error rate, and power:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.norm.test(d = .5, 
              n = NULL, 
              sig.level = .05, 
              power = .8,
              alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Mean power calculation for normal distribution with known variance 

              d = 0.5
              n = 31.39544
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided
```


:::
:::


## Power for $z$-tests

The `pwr` package also includes a plotting method. This means that we can use the function `plot()` with the output from any power calculation results. (they don't look very attractive)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(pwr.norm.test(d = .5, 
              n = 10, 
              sig.level = .05, 
              power = NULL,
              alternative = "two.sided"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Power_Analysis_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::



## One-sample $t$-test

In lab 4 we ran a one sample *t*-test to test whether average restaurant ratings were significantly different from 3. with $d = .21$ and $N = 200$ we can do a retrospective power calculation: 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t.test(n = 200, 
           d = .21, 
           sig.level = .05, 
           power = NULL, 
           type = "one.sample", 
           alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     One-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 200
              d = 0.21
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8402593
    alternative = two.sided
```


:::
:::


Our power was around .84. What does this mean?

## One-sample $t$-test

What if I want to repeat the previous "experiment", and I want to know the sample size that I would need to have .8, .9, and .95 power?

::: panel-tabset

## power = .80



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t.test(n = NULL, d = .21, sig.level = .05, power = .80,
           type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     One-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 179.9089
              d = 0.21
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided
```


:::
:::


## power = .90


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t.test(n = NULL, d = .21, sig.level = .05, power = .90,
           type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     One-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 240.1924
              d = 0.21
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9
    alternative = two.sided
```


:::
:::


## power = .95


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t.test(n = NULL, d = .21, sig.level = .05, power = .95,
           type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     One-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 296.5928
              d = 0.21
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.95
    alternative = two.sided
```


:::
:::


:::

For a priori power analysis, we want to round up, so $N = 180, 241, 297$ for 80%, 90%, and 95% power.

## Paired-samples $t$-test

Power analysis for a paired-sample *t*-test is the same as the one-sample $t$-test. Remember that you will output the number of **pairs** that you need. 

## Independent-samples $t$-test

For the independent samples $t$-test, we can use `pwr.t.test` if we have equal sample sizes, or `pwr.t2n.test` for unequal sample sizes. 

In the case of lab 4, where we were testing whether males ($n_{1} = 112$) and females ($n_{2} = 82$) were significantly different on average food rating. the estimate effect was $d = .17$, but the difference was not significant, $p = .224$. In retrospect, their power to detect an effect was only .21! 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t2n.test(n1 = 112, n2 = 82, d = .17, sig.level = .05,
             power = NULL, alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     t test power calculation 

             n1 = 112
             n2 = 82
              d = 0.17
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.2138687
    alternative = two.sided
```


:::
:::




## Independent-samples $t$-test

When planning data collection, plan for equally sized groups if possible because this maximizes power. Let's calculate a priori power assuming equal sample sizes and $d = .17$. 

::: panel-tabset

## power = .80


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t.test(n = NULL, d = .17, sig.level = .05, power = .80,
           type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 544.1358
              d = 0.17
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group
```


:::
:::


## power = .90


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t.test(n = NULL, d = .17, sig.level = .05, power = .90,
           type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 728.1188
              d = 0.17
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group
```


:::
:::


## power = .95


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.t.test(n = NULL, d = .17, sig.level = .05, power = .95,
           type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 900.2493
              d = 0.17
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.95
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group
```


:::
:::


:::

It turns out that $n$ = 545, 729, and 901 (quite large!) are the minimum sample sizes **in each group** for 80%, 90%, and 95% power.

## Power for $\chi^2$ tests

We can do the same for $\chi^2$ tests using the `pwr.chi.test` function. The test does not distinguish between $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit and $\chi^2$ test of independence. 

Let's use the airplane delays example from Lab 3. $\chi^2(1) = 4.2$ with $N = 1100$. Our $W$ coefficient was $.06$. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.chisq.test(w = .06, N = 1100, df = 1, sig.level = .05, power = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Chi squared power calculation 

              w = 0.06
              N = 1100
             df = 1
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.5120099

NOTE: N is the number of observations
```


:::
:::


Power is about .51 to detect such a small effect. 

## Power for $\chi^2$ tests

Finally, let's conduct a priori power for this study.

::: panel-tabset 

## power = 80


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.chisq.test(w = .06, N = NULL, df = 1, 
               sig.level = .05, power = .80)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Chi squared power calculation 

              w = 0.06
              N = 2180.239
             df = 1
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8

NOTE: N is the number of observations
```


:::
:::


## power = .90


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.chisq.test(w = .06, N = NULL, df = 1, 
               sig.level = .05, power = .90)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Chi squared power calculation 

              w = 0.06
              N = 2918.728
             df = 1
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9

NOTE: N is the number of observations
```


:::
:::


## power = .95 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pwr.chisq.test(w = .06, N = NULL, df = 1, 
               sig.level = .05, power = .95)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Chi squared power calculation 

              w = 0.06
              N = 3609.641
             df = 1
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.95

NOTE: N is the number of observations
```


:::
:::


:::
For this effect size, we would need data on $N = 2181, 2919, 3610$ flights for 80%, 90%, and 95% power.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
